Study of Bunsen burner Bunsen burner is commonly used heating device in laboratory. It was discovered by a German Scientist Robert Bunsen in 1855 . It can produce a high temperature up to 35000C.
It mainly consists of the following three parts:

Base: It is made of cast iron. It is heavy and keeps the burner in Upright position. It has a side tube that communicates inside with a jet. The base is connected to the gas tap through a rubber tube.
Barrel or chimney: It is metallic tube having a pair of air holes at the opposite sides near the lower end.
Air regulator or collar: It is fitted to the lower end of the barrel. It is used to close or open the air holes.
Practical Chemistry The burner burns with a mixture of fuel gas and air. Depending upon the quantity of air mixed, two types of flame can be seen.
1. With air holes closed: If the air holes are kept closed and the
burner is lighted, it gives a yellow and smoky flame, called the luminous flame (or, reducing flame).
2. With air holes opened: If the air holes are slowly opened,

smoky flame gradually disappears and non-luminous (or oxidising) flame is produced. This is the normal flame of the burner. This flame is used for heating purposes. This flame consists of two parts: inner blue part and outer hottest part.
